column9: stem
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: In a 3-D model of an animal cell, a student uses a walnut to stand for the part of the cell that holds the DNA and directs the cell's activities. Which cell part is the walnut?
column28: The nucleus holds the cell's DNA and controls the cell's activities, so it is the part the walnut represents. Ribosomes build proteins, the vacuole stores materials, and the cell membrane is the outer boundary. A common mistake is picking the cell membrane because it 'controls' what goes in and out, but that is not the same as directing the whole cell.
column29: Where are the cell's instructions (DNA) kept in a plant or animal cell?

column9: The organelle that assembles proteins, often shown as tiny dots in a cell model, is the ___.
column28: Ribosomes assemble (build) proteins. They are so small and so numerous that models show them as dots or sprinkles. Students sometimes write nucleolus; the nucleolus makes ribosomes, but the ribosome itself builds the protein.
column29: It is the tiniest organelle in your notes, and cells have thousands of them.

column9: Which structure surrounds every cell and controls what enters and leaves it?
column28: The cell membrane surrounds every cell and controls what moves in and out. The cell wall is a stiff layer found only in some cells (plants, fungi, bacteria), the nuclear membrane surrounds just the nucleus, and the central vacuole is a storage sac. A common mistake is choosing the cell wall because it is on the outside, but it is not found in every cell.
column29: The question says EVERY cell. Which choice do animal cells and plant cells both have on the outside?

column9: The jelly-like material that fills a cell and surrounds the organelles is the ___.
column28: Cytoplasm is the jelly-like material that supports and protects the organelles. A common mix-up is writing cytoskeleton, which is the network of protein fibers inside the cytoplasm.
column29: Its name starts with cyto- (cell), and it fills the space between the membrane and the nucleus.

column9: Which organelle captures energy from sunlight and uses it to make sugar?
column28: Chloroplasts capture energy from sunlight and store it in sugar (photosynthesis). Mitochondria do the opposite job: they break down sugar to release usable energy (ATP). Students often confuse the two because both deal with energy.
column29: This organelle is green and is found in leaf cells.

column9: In a cell model, a student labels a tiny sac "clean-up crew: breaks down worn-out parts and trash." Which organelle is it most likely?
column28: Lysosomes are sacs of digestive enzymes that break down particles and old cell parts. Ribosomes build proteins, the nucleolus makes ribosomes, and chloroplasts make sugar. A common mistake is picking the ribosome because the names sound alike.
column29: Which organelle is filled with digestive enzymes?

column9: In a clay cell model, a student shapes a stack of flattened, curved sacs, like a short stack of pancakes, sitting near the nucleus. Which organelle is the student most likely modeling?
column28: The Golgi apparatus looks like a stack of flattened, curved sacs. It modifies, packages, and labels proteins. Mitochondria are bean-shaped, ribosomes are tiny dots, and the nucleolus is a dark spot inside the nucleus. A common mistake is mixing it up with the rough ER, which is a folded maze of membranes attached to the nucleus rather than a separate stack.
column29: This organelle packages and labels proteins before they are shipped.

column9: A student models an organelle as a bean-shaped capsule with a folded inner membrane drawn inside it. The label says "makes ATP." Which organelle is this?
column28: Mitochondria are bean-shaped with a folded inner membrane, and they release usable energy (ATP) from food. Chloroplasts are also oval, but they are green and make sugar from sunlight instead. Students often swap the two energy organelles.
column29: Which organelle is called the powerhouse of the cell?

column9: The Golgi apparatus is found in both plant cells and animal cells.
column28: True. Both plant and animal cells make and ship proteins, so both have a Golgi apparatus. Only a few structures, like the cell wall, chloroplasts, and the large central vacuole, are plant-only. A common mistake is thinking every organelle belongs to just one cell type.
column29: Do plant cells need to package and ship proteins too?

column9: Ribosomes are surrounded by their own membrane.
column28: False. Ribosomes have no membrane; they are tiny clusters of RNA and protein. That is why even bacteria, which have no membrane-bound organelles, still have ribosomes. A common mistake is assuming every structure inside a cell is wrapped in a membrane.
column29: Even bacteria, which have no membrane-bound organelles, have ribosomes.

column9: What is the main job of the cell wall in a plant cell?
column15: It captures sunlight to make sugar
column16: It supports and protects the cell
column28: The cell wall is the rigid outer structure of plant cells (and bacteria and fungi). It gives the cell support and protection. Building proteins is the ribosomes' job, DNA is stored in the nucleus, and chloroplasts capture sunlight. A common mistake is thinking the wall controls what enters and leaves; that is the cell membrane's job.
column29: Think about why a plant can stand up tall without a skeleton.

column9: A student models an animal cell as a rounded, flexible blob instead of a rectangle. Why is that shape reasonable?
column14: Animal cells are always perfect circles
column15: Animal cells have a round cell wall
column16: Animal cells have no cell membrane, so nothing holds a shape
column17: Animal cells have only a flexible membrane on the outside, so their shape can be rounded or irregular
column28: Animal cells have a flexible cell membrane but no rigid cell wall, so they can be rounded or irregular. Plant cells look boxy because of their cell wall. A common mistake is thinking animal cells are perfect circles; many, like nerve cells, have very different shapes.
column29: What stiff structure gives plant cells their boxy shape? Do animal cells have it?

column9: Which organelle should a model show as a folded system of membranes connected directly to the nucleus?
column28: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a folded system of membranes that connects to the nuclear membrane and transports materials through the cell. The cell wall is on the outside, the central vacuole is a storage sac, and a flagellum sticks out of the cell. A common mistake is placing the ER far from the nucleus in a model.
column29: Which organelle transports materials and comes in rough and smooth forms?

column9: Which structure makes the cell's ribosomes?
column28: The nucleolus, the dark spot inside the nucleus, is where ribosomes are made. Vesicles carry materials, lysosomes digest, and the Golgi packages proteins. Students sometimes confuse the nucleolus with the nucleus; the nucleolus is a smaller region inside it.
column29: Its name sounds like a smaller version of "nucleus."

column9: The ___ is a network of protein fibers that helps a cell keep its shape and moves organelles around.
column28: The cytoskeleton is made of structural protein fibers that help the cell keep its shape. A common mistake is writing cytoplasm, which is the jelly the fibers sit in, or cell wall, which is an outer layer found only in some cells.
column29: Like the poles inside a tent, it is a support frame on the INSIDE of the cell. The word starts with cyto-.

column9: Cells lining your windpipe have many short, hair-like projections that beat together to sweep mucus and dust up toward your throat. What are these structures?
column28: Cilia are short, hair-like projections, usually many on one cell, that beat to move things past the cell. Flagella are long, whip-like tails, usually one or a few per cell, used for swimming. Students often mix them up; remember cilia are short and many.
column29: Short and many, or long and few?

column9: A human sperm cell swims using one long, whip-like tail. What is this structure called?
column28: A flagellum is a long, whip-like tail used for swimming, and a sperm cell has one. Cilia are short hairs, and there are usually many of them. A common mistake is calling any moving structure cilia.
column29: Is it a short hair or one long whip?

column9: What is the main job of the nuclear membrane?
column14: It controls what moves into and out of the nucleus
column28: The nuclear membrane (nuclear envelope) surrounds the nucleus and controls movement in and out of it through small pores. Making ribosomes is the nucleolus's job. A common mistake is confusing the nuclear membrane with the nucleolus because both are part of the nucleus.
column29: A membrane is a boundary. What would a boundary around the nucleus do?

column9: Looking at Elodea (a pond plant) leaf cells under a microscope, a student sees many small green ovals moving around the edges of each cell. What are the green ovals?
column28: The green ovals are chloroplasts; they are green because they contain chlorophyll. Mitochondria are hard to see with a classroom light microscope and are not green. A common mistake is calling them nuclei, but each cell has only one nucleus.
column29: Which organelle is green?

column9: A student scrapes cells from the inside of her cheek, stains them with methylene blue, and sees one dark-stained round spot in the middle of each cell. What is the spot most likely?
column28: The stain colors DNA strongly, so the dark round spot is the nucleus. Cheek cells are animal cells, so they have no cell wall, chloroplasts, or central vacuole. A common mistake is choosing a plant-only structure because it was seen in an earlier plant-cell lab.
column29: Cheek cells are animal cells. Which choice do animal cells actually have?

column9: A student needs a material for the cell membrane in a 3-D model. Which choice best shows how a real cell membrane behaves?
column15: A plastic tackle box with dividers
column28: A thin balloon is flexible, like the cell membrane. The box, jar, and tackle box are rigid, which fits a cell wall better. A common mistake is choosing a sturdy container because it 'holds everything in,' but being flexible is what separates the membrane from the wall.
column29: Which choice can bend and change shape?

column9: For a 3-D model of a plant cell, which material would best represent the cell wall?
column14: A stiff cardboard box around the whole model
column28: The cell wall is a rigid outer layer that gives support, so a stiff box around the model fits. String and spaghetti are floppy, and a jelly bean is too small and isn't around the outside. A common mistake is using something flexible, which better represents the cell membrane.
column29: Is the cell wall stiff or floppy? Where is it located?

column9: In most diagrams of a mature plant cell, which structure takes up the most space?
column28: The large central vacuole stores water, food, and waste, and in a mature plant cell it can fill most of the cell, pushing the other organelles to the edges. A common mistake is choosing the nucleus, which is large but much smaller than a full central vacuole.
column29: This plant structure is a big storage tank for water.

column9: What are the small membrane bubbles that carry materials from one part of a cell to another?
column28: Vesicles are small membrane sacs that carry materials, for example from the ER to the Golgi and from the Golgi to the cell membrane. Ribosomes have no membrane, and cilia stick out from the cell surface. A common mistake is choosing ribosomes because they are also small and numerous.
column29: These little 'delivery bubbles' bud off the Golgi apparatus.

column9: In a correct model of a plant or animal cell, where should the DNA be placed?
column28: Plant and animal cells are eukaryotic, so their DNA is kept inside the nucleus. DNA floating loose in the cytoplasm is how prokaryotes (bacteria) store it. A common mistake is drawing the DNA loose, like in a bacterial cell model.
column29: What does "eukaryotic" tell you about where the DNA is kept?

column9: Put these structures in order from the outermost layer of a plant cell inward to the nucleolus.
column28: From outside in: cell wall → cell membrane → cytoplasm → nuclear membrane → nucleolus. The wall is outside the membrane, and the nucleolus sits inside the nucleus. A common mistake is putting the cell membrane outside the cell wall.
column29: Which boundary is stiff and outermost? Which tiny structure sits inside the nucleus?

column9: Which of these cells can use light energy to make its own sugar?
column14: A cell from a maple leaf
column28: A maple leaf cell has chloroplasts, which use light to make sugar. Human, dog, and frog cells are animal cells, which have no chloroplasts and must get sugar from food. A common mistake is thinking any cell with mitochondria can make sugar; mitochondria break sugar down instead.
column29: Which organism is a plant?

column9: A student compares a cell to a smartphone. Which cell part best matches the battery that supplies the energy every app needs to run?
column28: Mitochondria release usable energy (ATP) that powers the cell's work, just like a battery powers every app. The cell wall supports, the vacuole stores, and the nucleolus makes ribosomes. A common mistake is choosing the nucleus or nucleolus because they seem 'in charge,' but being in charge is not the same as supplying energy.
column29: Which organelle releases the energy the cell uses?

column9: A cell is compared to a pizza restaurant. Which cell part best matches the recipe book that holds the instructions for every item on the menu?
column28: The nucleus holds DNA, the cell's set of instructions, just like a recipe book holds the instructions for each pizza. A common mistake is choosing the ribosome because it 'makes' things, but it follows instructions; it doesn't store them.
column29: Where are the cell's instructions stored?

column9: A student compares a cell to a pizza restaurant. The cooks follow recipes to put pizzas together from ingredients. Which cell part do the cooks best represent?
column28: Ribosomes follow the DNA's instructions to assemble proteins from amino acids, like cooks building pizzas from ingredients. A common mistake is choosing the nucleus because it is the most famous organelle, but the nucleus stores the instructions rather than doing the building.
column29: Which organelle assembles proteins?

column9: A student compares a cell to a post office. Which cell part best matches the sorting room where packages are labeled and sent to the right address?
column28: The Golgi apparatus modifies, packages, and labels proteins and sends them where they need to go, just like a post office sorting room. Mitochondria supply energy, the cell wall gives support, and the nucleolus makes ribosomes. A common mistake is choosing a part that 'directs' things, like the nucleolus.
column29: Which organelle packages and labels proteins?

column9: A student builds a model where 1 µm of real cell is shown as 3 cm. A real mitochondrion is 2 µm long. How long, in cm, should the model mitochondrion be?
column28: 2 µm × 3 cm per µm = 6 cm. Every real micrometer becomes 3 cm in the model. A common mistake is adding (2 + 3 = 5) instead of multiplying.
column29: Each 1 µm becomes 3 cm. How many µm long is the mitochondrion?

column9: A student's cell model uses red beads, green clay ovals, and a blue balloon for different cell parts. What is the purpose of adding a key (legend) to the model?
column14: It makes the model look more colorful
column15: It tells the viewer which color or material stands for each cell part
column16: It shows how big the real cell is
column17: It explains where the student bought the materials
column28: A key (legend) explains what each color or material represents, so anyone can read the model. Real size is shown with a scale, not a key. A common mistake is thinking a key is decoration; without it, viewers have to guess what each bead or color means.
column29: Think of the key on a map. What does it tell you?

column9: Why do biologists and students build models of cells?
column14: Models are always exactly the same as real cells
column15: Real cells do not have any organelles
column16: Cells and their parts are too small to see in detail, so a model shows the structures and how they fit together
column17: Models let you watch a real cell grow
column28: Most cells and organelles are too small to see without a microscope, so models make the structures big enough to see, compare, and explain. No model is exactly like the real thing. A common mistake is thinking a model must be perfect to be useful.
column29: What makes studying a real cell difficult without help?

column9: Select every structure found in BOTH plant cells and animal cells. Select all that apply.
column28: Both plant and animal cells have a nucleus, mitochondria, and a cell membrane. The cell wall, chloroplasts, and large central vacuole are found in plant cells. A common mistake is leaving out mitochondria for plants; plants need them to release energy from the sugar they make.
column29: Three of these are plant-only. The other three are needed by both.

column9: Which of these cells has a cell wall?
column28: Cell walls are found in plants, bacteria, and fungi. E. coli is a bacterium, so it has a cell wall. Human, frog, and dog cells are animal cells, which have only a cell membrane on the outside. A common mistake is thinking only plants have cell walls.
column29: Animal cells never have a cell wall. Which choice is not an animal cell?

column9: Which of these can count as a scientific model of a cell?
column14: A labeled drawing, a clay model, or a computer animation can all be models
column15: Only a 3-D model made of clay
column16: Only a photograph of a real cell
column17: Only a model made from real cell material
column28: A model is any representation that helps explain how something is built or works, so drawings, 3-D models, and animations all count. A photo is evidence, not a model you create. A common mistake is thinking only 3-D projects count as models.
column29: A model is anything that represents the real thing to help explain it.

column9: Which feature makes a cell model the most scientifically useful?
column14: It is as large as possible
column15: Its parts are labeled correctly and placed where they belong in the cell
column16: It shows only the nucleus so it stays simple
column17: It uses as many colors as possible
column28: A useful model shows the right parts, with correct labels, in the right places. Color and size can help, but they don't make a model accurate. A common mistake is focusing on how the model looks instead of whether it is correct.
column29: Would a colorful model with wrong labels help anyone learn?

column9: Which structure should appear the MOST times in an accurate model of a typical animal cell?
column28: A cell has thousands to millions of ribosomes, so they should appear far more often than anything else. A typical cell has one nucleus and one cell membrane. A common mistake is drawing just a few ribosomes because they are small.
column29: Which of these is tiny and found by the thousands?

column9: In a correct model of an animal cell, where should the ribosomes be placed?
column14: Only on the outside of the cell membrane
column17: Floating in the cytoplasm and attached to the rough ER
column28: Ribosomes are found free in the cytoplasm and attached to the rough ER, where they build proteins. They are made in the nucleolus but work outside the nucleus. A common mistake is putting them only in the nucleus because that is where they are made.
column29: Where in the cell are proteins built?

column9: The cell membrane is made mostly of which molecules?
column28: The cell membrane is a double layer of phospholipids, a type of lipid from Unit 2, with proteins scattered in it. Cellulose, chlorophyll, and starch are made by plants but do not form the membrane. A common mistake is mixing up what the membrane and the cell wall are made of.
column29: Think back to Unit 2: which macromolecule makes up membranes?

column9: Plant cell walls are made mainly of which carbohydrate?
column28: Plant cell walls are made mainly of cellulose, a tough carbohydrate built from glucose. Starch is how plants store sugar, glycogen is how animals store it, and chitin is found in fungi and insect shells. A common mistake is choosing starch because it is also a plant carbohydrate.
column29: It is the fiber in celery and the main part of paper and wood.

column9: Which job belongs to the smooth endoplasmic reticulum?
column16: Making lipids, such as the phospholipids in membranes
column28: Smooth ER has no ribosomes; it makes lipids. Building proteins happens on the rough ER, where ribosomes are attached. A common mistake is thinking both kinds of ER do the same job.
column29: Smooth ER has no ribosomes. So which job can it NOT do, and what is left?

column9: A student's model shows a cell with a cell wall and chloroplasts. What type of cell is the student most likely modeling?
column28: Chloroplasts plus a cell wall point to a plant cell. Animal (and human) cells have neither, and bacteria have a cell wall but no chloroplasts. A common mistake is choosing bacterial cell because bacteria have walls, but bacteria have no membrane-bound organelles like chloroplasts.
column29: Which cell type has BOTH of these structures?

column9: Which cell part stores water, food, and waste?
column28: Vacuoles store water, food, and waste. Plant cells have one large central vacuole; animal cells have small ones, if any. Ribosomes build proteins, the nucleolus makes ribosomes, and the cytoskeleton gives shape. A common mistake is choosing the nucleolus because both names have a similar sound.
column29: Think of a storage tank or closet in the cell.

column9: A student builds a cell model on a round cake. Near the center is a large round cookie. Next to the cookie, a strip of fruit leather is folded back and forth and covered with sprinkles. Which structure does the sprinkled fruit leather most likely represent?
column28: A folded membrane system next to the nucleus, dotted with ribosomes (the sprinkles), is the rough ER. Smooth ER has the same folded shape but no ribosomes. The Golgi is a separate stack of sacs that is not covered with ribosomes. A common mistake is choosing smooth ER because of forgetting what the sprinkles stand for.
column29: What do the sprinkles probably stand for, and which organelle is covered in them?

column9: A student's plant cell model contains 1 nucleus, 6 chloroplasts, 4 mitochondria, 1 central vacuole, and 20 ribosomes. How many of these structures are membrane-bound organelles?
column28: Nucleus (1) + chloroplasts (6) + mitochondria (4) + central vacuole (1) = 12. Ribosomes have no membrane, so the 20 ribosomes do not count. A common mistake is adding everything (32) or counting ribosomes as membrane-bound.
column29: Which item on the list is NOT surrounded by a membrane?

column9: A student's model of a mature leaf cell shows the nucleus in the exact center and a small central vacuole squeezed into one corner. What is the best correction?
column14: Move the nucleus outside the cell membrane
column15: Replace the nucleus with loose DNA
column16: Make the central vacuole large so it fills most of the cell and pushes the nucleus toward the edge
column17: Remove the central vacuole, because plant cells don't have one
column28: In a mature plant cell, the large central vacuole stores water and fills most of the cell, so the nucleus and other organelles are pushed toward the edges. Plant cells do have a central vacuole, and the nucleus always stays inside the cell. A common mistake is drawing a plant cell like an animal cell with a tiny vacuole.
column29: In a mature plant cell, which structure is the biggest?

column9: A diagram of a human sperm cell shows its middle section packed with mitochondria, right where the flagellum attaches. What is the best explanation for this?
column14: Mitochondria make the sugar the sperm cell eats
column15: The mitochondria store the DNA the sperm delivers
column16: Mitochondria make the flagellum stiff like a cell wall
column17: The flagellum needs a large supply of ATP to keep beating as the sperm swims
column28: Mitochondria release usable energy (ATP), and a beating flagellum uses a lot of it. Packing mitochondria next to the flagellum puts the energy supply where it is needed. A common mistake is thinking mitochondria make sugar; chloroplasts make sugar, and mitochondria break it down. The sperm's DNA is in its nucleus, in the head.
column29: What does a flagellum need in order to keep moving, and which organelle supplies it?

column9: In Tay-Sachs disease, one digestive enzyme is missing from a certain organelle. Fatty materials that should be broken down build up inside nerve cells instead. Which organelle is not working correctly?
column28: Lysosomes hold the digestive enzymes that break down particles and old cell parts. When one lysosome enzyme is missing, the material it should digest builds up. Chloroplasts and central vacuoles aren't found in human nerve cells, and the nucleolus makes ribosomes. A common mistake is choosing the vacuole because it stores things, but the problem is breakdown, not storage.
column29: Which organelle works like the cell's digestive system?

column9: Liver cells make lipids and break down alcohol, medicines, and other harmful chemicals. Which organelle would you expect a model of a liver cell to show a lot of?
column28: Smooth ER makes lipids and, in liver cells, helps break down alcohol, drugs, and other toxins, so liver cells have lots of it. Liver cells are animal cells, so they have no chloroplasts or cell wall, and cilia are for sweeping or swimming. A common mistake is choosing rough ER or ribosomes, which make proteins rather than lipids.
column29: Which organelle makes lipids?

column9: Smoking damages the cilia on the cells lining the airways. Which problem would most likely result?
column15: The cells can no longer make proteins
column16: Mucus and trapped dirt are not swept out of the airways as well, so smokers cough more
column17: The cells start to make their own sugar
column28: Cilia beat to sweep mucus, dust, and germs up and out of the airways. When cilia are damaged, mucus builds up, and the body coughs to clear it. Making proteins is the ribosomes' job, and losing cilia doesn't remove the nucleus. A common mistake is thinking cilia help cells breathe; they move things past the cell.
column29: What job do airway cilia normally do?

column9: A mature human red blood cell has no nucleus. Which statement best describes a result of this?
column14: It has a cell wall instead
column15: It makes more proteins than other cells
column16: It can make sugar using sunlight
column17: It has more room to carry oxygen, but it cannot divide to make new cells
column28: Without a nucleus, there is more space for hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein, but the cell has no DNA instructions, so it can't divide or repair itself. That's why red blood cells only last about 120 days. A common mistake is thinking the cell would make more proteins; without DNA instructions it can't make new ones.
column29: The nucleus holds the DNA instructions. What can a cell not do without them?

column9: Salivary gland cells make amylase, an enzyme (a protein) that is released into your saliva. Put the steps in order, from first to last.
column14: A vesicle carries amylase to the cell membrane and releases it outside the cell
column15: Instructions for amylase leave the nucleus
column16: Ribosomes on the rough ER build the amylase protein
column17: The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages amylase
column18: A vesicle carries amylase from the ER to the Golgi apparatus
column28: Nucleus (instructions) → ribosomes on rough ER (build the protein) → vesicle to the Golgi → Golgi (modify and package) → vesicle to the cell membrane (release). A common mistake is putting the Golgi before the ER; the protein must be built before it can be packaged.
column29: A protein must be built before it can be packaged, and packaged before it is shipped.

column9: Put these from smallest to largest.
column14: The nucleus of a cheek cell
column28: Ribosome (about 0.025 µm) → mitochondrion (about 1 to 2 µm) → nucleus (about 5 to 10 µm) → whole cheek cell (about 50 µm). A common mistake is placing the mitochondrion above the nucleus; a cell holds hundreds of mitochondria but only one nucleus, which is much larger.
column29: Which one is so small that thousands fit in a cell? Which one contains all the others?

column9: Select every structure you would expect to see in an accurate model of a cell from an onion bulb (the part we eat). Select all that apply.
column28: An onion bulb cell is a plant cell, so it has a cell wall, a large central vacuole, a nucleus, and mitochondria. The bulb grows underground and stores food rather than making it, so its cells have no chloroplasts. Plant cells don't have flagella. A common mistake is adding chloroplasts to every plant cell.
column29: Is the onion bulb in sunlight? Does it make its own food?

column9: A student looks at onion skin cells and sees boxy outlines around each cell but no green structures. She concludes they must be animal cells. What is the best response?
column14: They are still plant cells; the boxy outline is the cell wall, and not every plant cell has chloroplasts
column15: She is right, because all plant cells have chloroplasts
column16: She is right, because animal cells have boxy outlines
column17: They are bacteria, because they have cell walls
column28: The rigid, boxy outline is the cell wall, which animal cells never have. Onion bulb cells don't get light, so they have no chloroplasts, but they are still plant cells. A common mistake is using chloroplasts as the only test for a plant cell.
column29: Which structure makes the boxy outline? Do animal cells have it?

column9: A classmate says plant cells don't need mitochondria because their chloroplasts already take care of energy. Which statement corrects this?
column14: Chloroplasts make ATP for the whole cell, so mitochondria are found only in animals
column15: Chloroplasts make sugar, and mitochondria break that sugar down to release ATP, so plant cells need both
column16: Mitochondria make sugar at night when chloroplasts can't
column17: Plant cells use their cell wall to make ATP
column28: Chloroplasts capture light energy and store it in sugar. Mitochondria then break down that sugar to release ATP the cell can use, day and night. So plant cells have both. A common mistake is thinking mitochondria are animal-only.
column29: Making sugar and using sugar are two different jobs. Which organelle does each?

column9: A student draws a flat poster of a cell. The cell membrane is a thick black line, and every organelle is drawn locked in one spot. Which is a limitation of this model?
column14: The poster should not show a cell membrane at all
column15: Real organelles are glued to the cell membrane
column16: Real cells are 3-D, the membrane is thin and flexible, and organelles can move around in the cytoplasm
column17: A poster can never be a scientific model
column28: All models have limits. A flat drawing can't show that a cell is 3-D, that the membrane is thin and flexible, or that organelles move through the cytoplasm. That doesn't make the poster useless; it just has limits. A common mistake is thinking a model with limits isn't a model at all.
column29: Compare the poster to a real living cell. What can't a flat, still picture show?

column9: A student compares a cell to a car. Which pairing is the BEST match?
column14: Ribosomes = the fuel tank, because they store energy
column15: Cell wall = the steering wheel, because it directs the cell
column16: Nucleus = the seat belts, because it holds organelles in place
column17: Mitochondria = the engine, because they supply the energy that makes everything run
column28: Mitochondria release usable energy (ATP), like an engine turning fuel into power. The cell wall supports and protects (more like the car's frame), ribosomes build proteins, and the nucleus holds the instructions (more like the driver). A common mistake is choosing an analogy because the words sound connected, without checking the job.
column29: Match jobs, not names. Which car part provides the power?

column9: A student compares a plant cell to a house. Which cell part best matches the wooden frame inside the walls that holds the house in shape?
column28: The cytoskeleton is a network of protein fibers INSIDE the cell that helps it keep its shape, like a house's inner frame. The cell wall is outside the membrane, more like the house's outer siding or a fence. A common mistake is picking the cell wall because both give support, but the question says the frame is inside.
column29: The frame is on the INSIDE. Which support structure is inside the cell?

column9: A student compares a plant cell to a farm. Match each cell part to the farm part that does a similar job.
column14: Chloroplast :: Solar panels on the barn roof that capture sunlight
column15: Cell wall :: The stone wall around the farm that supports and protects
column16: Central vacuole :: The water tower that stores water
column17: Nucleus :: The farm office that holds the plans and gives directions
column18: Mitochondria :: The generator that turns fuel into usable power
column28: Chloroplasts capture light (solar panels), the cell wall supports and protects (stone wall), the central vacuole stores water (water tower), the nucleus holds the instructions (office), and mitochondria release usable energy (generator). Students often swap the solar panels and the generator; one captures sunlight, the other turns fuel into power.
column29: Match on the job: capturing light, protecting, storing, directing, or powering.

column9: In a cell model, 1 µm of real cell is shown as 2 cm. The model chloroplast is 10 cm long. How long is the real chloroplast, in µm?
column28: Divide the model size by the scale: 10 cm ÷ 2 cm per µm = 5 µm. A common mistake is multiplying (10 × 2 = 20), which goes the wrong direction; the real chloroplast must be smaller than the model.
column29: Going from the model back to the real cell, should the number get bigger or smaller?

column9: A real animal cell is 20 µm wide, and its nucleus is 5 µm wide. A student's model cell is 40 cm wide. To keep the same scale, how wide should the model nucleus be, in cm?
column28: The scale is 40 cm ÷ 20 µm = 2 cm per µm, so the nucleus is 5 µm × 2 = 10 cm. Another way: the nucleus is 1/4 as wide as the cell, and 1/4 of 40 cm is 10 cm. A common mistake is just using 5 cm, which makes the nucleus too small for this model.
column29: How many cm of model stand for each µm of real cell?

column9: A student wants viewers to be able to tell the rough ER apart from the smooth ER in a model. Which choice does this best?
column14: Put the rough ER outside the cell membrane
column15: Stick small beads (ribosomes) on the rough ER and leave the smooth ER bare
column16: Color the smooth ER green because it makes sugar
column17: Make the smooth ER bigger than the nucleus
column28: The difference between them is ribosomes: rough ER is studded with ribosomes, and smooth ER has none. Beads on one and not the other shows that clearly. Neither type makes sugar, and both are inside the cell. A common mistake is thinking 'rough' and 'smooth' describe a texture you could feel rather than the ribosomes.
column29: What makes rough ER look rough?

column9: In microscope images, most plant cells look like boxy rectangles, while many animal cells look rounded or irregular. What is the main reason?
column16: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall that holds a fixed shape
column17: Plant cells have a nucleus and animal cells do not
column28: The rigid cell wall gives plant cells their boxy shape. Animal cells have only a flexible membrane, so they can take many shapes. Both cell types have a nucleus and cytoplasm. A common mistake is crediting the cell membrane, which is flexible in both.
column29: Which plant-only structure is stiff?

column9: A typical human cheek cell is about 50 µm wide. About how many cheek cells, lined up side by side, would stretch across 1 mm? (1 mm = 1,000 µm)
column28: 1 mm = 1,000 µm, and 1,000 µm ÷ 50 µm = 20 cells. That's why you need a microscope to see them. A common mistake is dividing 50 by 1 without converting millimeters to micrometers.
column29: Change 1 mm into µm first, then divide by the size of one cell.

column9: Which observation would BEST show that a cell in a microscope image is a plant cell rather than an animal cell?
column17: It has a boxy cell wall and a large central vacuole
column28: A cell wall and a large central vacuole are found in plant cells, not animal cells. A nucleus, mitochondria, and a cell membrane are in both, so they can't tell the two apart. A common mistake is choosing a structure that is real but shared by both types.
column29: Pick a feature that only one of the two cell types has.

column9: Select every organelle that plays a part in making a protein and shipping it out of the cell. Select all that apply.
column28: Ribosomes build the protein, often on the rough ER; the ER moves it to the Golgi, which packages it; and vesicles carry it to the cell membrane. Chloroplasts make sugar, and the central vacuole stores water. A common mistake is leaving out vesicles, the small 'delivery bubbles' between the steps.
column29: Think build → package → ship. Which organelles do each step?

column9: Goblet cells in your intestines release large amounts of mucus out of the cell. The mucus must be packaged into vesicles before it leaves. Which organelle would be especially large in a goblet cell?
column28: The Golgi apparatus packages products into vesicles to be shipped out of the cell, so cells that release lots of mucus have a large Golgi. Lysosomes break things down, the nucleolus makes ribosomes, and the cytoskeleton gives shape. A common mistake is choosing lysosomes because they are also sacs, but they digest rather than ship.
column29: Which organelle packages materials for shipping?

column9: If a cell's nucleolus stopped working, what would the cell soon run short of?
column15: New ribosomes, and so the ability to make enough proteins
column28: The nucleolus makes ribosomes. Without new ribosomes, the cell would gradually be unable to build enough proteins. A common mistake is thinking the nucleolus holds all the cell's DNA; the DNA is in the nucleus, and the nucleolus is the ribosome-making region inside it.
column29: What does the nucleolus make?

column9: A student's model has a nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, ER, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, and a cell membrane, but no cell wall, no chloroplasts, and no large central vacuole. What type of cell is it most likely modeling?
column28: With a nucleus and organelles but no cell wall, chloroplasts, or large central vacuole, this is an animal cell. Every plant cell, including root cells, has a cell wall, and bacteria have no nucleus, ER, or Golgi. A common mistake is choosing a root cell because roots lack chloroplasts, but roots still have cell walls.
column29: Which cell type has no cell wall at all?

column9: In Elodea leaf cells, chloroplasts can be seen slowly moving in a circle around the cell. Which structures move them?
column15: The cell wall squeezing the cell
column16: Cilia on the outside of the cell
column17: Cytoskeleton fibers that move organelles through the cytoplasm
column28: The cytoskeleton is a network of protein fibers that helps the cell keep its shape and also moves organelles through the cytoplasm. The cell wall doesn't squeeze, and cilia are on the outside of some cells and move things past the cell. A common mistake is thinking the cytoskeleton only holds shape; it is also a set of tracks for moving organelles.
column29: Which network of fibers inside the cell works as both a frame and a set of tracks?

column9: Which statement about the cell membrane and the cell wall is correct?
column14: Every cell has a cell membrane, but only some cells (like plants, fungi, and bacteria) also have a cell wall
column15: Plant cells have a cell wall instead of a cell membrane
column16: Every cell has a cell wall, but only animal cells have a cell membrane
column17: The cell wall is inside the cell membrane
column28: All cells have a cell membrane. Plants, fungi, and bacteria also have a stiff cell wall outside the membrane. A common mistake is thinking plant cells have a wall INSTEAD of a membrane; they have both, with the wall on the outside.
column29: Do plant cells still need something that controls what enters and leaves?

column9: Match each specialized cell to the structure that best fits its job.
column14: A cell in a sunflower leaf :: Many chloroplasts
column15: A Paramecium swimming through pond water :: Many cilia
column16: A liver cell that breaks down toxins :: Lots of smooth ER
column17: A cell that releases mucus :: A large Golgi apparatus
column28: Leaf cells capture sunlight with chloroplasts, a Paramecium swims with cilia, liver cells use smooth ER to break down toxins, and mucus cells package mucus in a large Golgi. A common mistake is matching the liver cell to the Golgi; breaking down toxins is a smooth ER job.
column29: For each cell, ask what its main job is, then which organelle does that job.

column9: Two students modeled the same spinach leaf cell. Model A shows one huge chloroplast in the center. Model B shows about 30 small chloroplasts spread around the edge of the cell, next to the membrane, with a large central vacuole in the middle. Which model is more accurate, and why?
column14: Model A, because a cell needs only one chloroplast
column15: Model B, because leaf cells have many chloroplasts that are pushed toward the edges by the large central vacuole
column16: Model B, because chloroplasts are glued to the cell wall and can never move
column17: Model A, because chloroplasts belong in the center of the cell like the nucleus
column28: Leaf cells hold dozens of chloroplasts, and the large central vacuole fills the middle, so the chloroplasts sit in the thin layer of cytoplasm near the edge. Model B is more accurate, but not because chloroplasts are glued in place; they move through the cytoplasm. A common mistake is picking the right model for the wrong reason.
column29: How many chloroplasts does a leaf cell have, and what fills the middle of a plant cell?

column9: A student draws a cell seen at 400× magnification. In the drawing, the cell is 20 mm wide. What is the cell's actual width, in µm? (1 mm = 1,000 µm)
column28: Actual size = drawing size ÷ magnification. 20 mm ÷ 400 = 0.05 mm, and 0.05 mm × 1,000 = 50 µm. A common mistake is multiplying by 400, which makes the real cell bigger than the drawing, or forgetting to convert mm to µm (answering 0.05).
column29: The real cell is much smaller than the drawing. Divide first, then convert mm to µm.

column9: A student builds a model in which a 25 µm cell becomes 50 cm wide. A ribosome is about 0.025 µm across. At this scale, how wide should the model ribosome be, in millimeters? (1 cm = 10 mm)
column28: Scale: 50 cm ÷ 25 µm = 2 cm per µm. Ribosome: 0.025 µm × 2 cm = 0.05 cm = 0.5 mm, about the size of a grain of sand. That's why sprinkles or dots are a good choice for ribosomes. A common mistake is stopping at 0.05 (that's in cm) and forgetting to convert to mm.
column29: First find how many cm stand for 1 µm. Then convert the ribosome's model size from cm to mm.

column9: Four students listed the parts in their models of a pea plant leaf cell. Which list is the most accurate?
column14: Cell membrane, nucleus, chloroplasts, mitochondria, ribosomes, ER, Golgi apparatus (no cell wall)
column15: Cell wall, cell membrane, chloroplasts, mitochondria, ribosomes, DNA loose in the cytoplasm (no nucleus)
column16: Cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus, chloroplasts, mitochondria, large central vacuole, ribosomes, ER, Golgi apparatus
column17: Cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus, chloroplasts, large central vacuole, ribosomes, ER, Golgi apparatus (no mitochondria)
column28: A leaf cell is a plant cell, so it needs everything a typical eukaryotic cell has (nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, ER, Golgi, membrane) plus a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole. The other lists leave out the mitochondria, the cell wall, or the nucleus. A common mistake is dropping mitochondria from plant cells.
column29: Check each list for the plant-only parts AND the parts every eukaryotic cell needs.

column9: A scientist describes the structures she found in five different cells. Match each description to the cell it most likely came from.
column14: Cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole :: A spinach leaf cell
column15: Cell wall and many starch-storing grains, but no chloroplasts :: A potato cell from underground
column16: No cell wall, a long tail for swimming, and many mitochondria :: A human sperm cell
column17: No cell wall and no nucleus, packed with hemoglobin :: A mature human red blood cell
column18: Cell wall and ribosomes, with DNA loose in the cytoplasm and no nucleus :: A bacterium
column28: Chloroplasts plus a wall and central vacuole point to a leaf cell; a wall with starch but no chloroplasts fits an underground potato cell; a swimming tail and many mitochondria fit a sperm cell; no nucleus and lots of hemoglobin is a red blood cell; and DNA loose in the cytoplasm is a bacterium. A common mistake is matching the potato to the leaf because both are plant cells; only one gets sunlight.
column29: First sort plant vs. animal vs. bacterium using the cell wall and nucleus. Then look at the special features.

column9: A drug stops a cell's Golgi apparatus from working. The ribosomes on the rough ER keep building a protein that is supposed to be sent out of the cell. What will most likely happen?
column14: The protein will be released faster because it skips a step
column15: The cell will stop making ATP
column16: The cell will begin making sugar instead
column17: The protein won't be finished, packaged, and shipped, so it builds up inside the cell instead of leaving
column28: The Golgi modifies, packages, and labels proteins and sends them off in vesicles. If it stops working, proteins pile up instead of being shipped out. Making ATP is the mitochondria's job. A common mistake is thinking that skipping a step makes things faster; without packaging, the protein never gets sent.
column29: What job does the Golgi do between the ER and the cell membrane?

column9: A student's animal cell model shows all of the ribosomes inside the nucleus, with none in the cytoplasm or on the ER. The student explains, "Ribosomes are made in the nucleus, so that's where they belong." What is the best evaluation?
column14: Ribosomes are made in the nucleolus, but they do their work in the cytoplasm and on the rough ER, so the model should show them there
column15: The model is correct, because ribosomes never leave the nucleus
column16: The model is correct, but the ribosomes should be inside the mitochondria instead
column17: The ribosomes should be removed, because animal cells don't have them
column28: The nucleolus makes ribosome parts, which then leave the nucleus. Ribosomes build proteins free in the cytoplasm and on the rough ER. Where something is made isn't always where it works. A common mistake is thinking animal cells lack ribosomes; every cell has them.
column29: Where is a ribosome made, and where does it build proteins? Are those the same place?

column9: A student says the cell membrane is like a brick wall. What is the biggest weakness of this analogy?
column14: A brick wall is made of bricks, but the membrane is made of cellulose
column15: A brick wall is rigid and blocks everything, but the membrane is flexible and lets some materials through while keeping others out
column16: There is no weakness; a brick wall is a perfect match
column17: A brick wall is outside a building, but the membrane is in the center of the cell
column28: The membrane is flexible and selectively permeable: it controls what enters and leaves. A brick wall is stiff and lets nothing through. The membrane is made of phospholipids, not cellulose. A common mistake is thinking every analogy is either perfect or useless; most have strengths and weaknesses.
column29: Does the membrane block everything? Is it stiff?

column9: Cells in the tip of a growing plant root divide often, and they must copy their DNA and build many new proteins. Which feature would a model of these cells most likely show?
column14: Many chloroplasts to make sugar underground
column15: No nucleus, to leave more room for growth
column16: A large nucleus with a large nucleolus, and many ribosomes
column17: A cell membrane but no cell wall
column28: Cells that build many proteins need lots of ribosomes, which come from the nucleolus, and dividing cells need a nucleus to copy their DNA. Root tips are underground, so no chloroplasts, and every plant cell has a cell wall. A common mistake is giving every plant cell chloroplasts or thinking a cell can grow and divide without its nucleus.
column29: Which structures does a cell need to make lots of proteins and to divide?

column9: Which statements describe correct placement in a model of a eukaryotic cell? Select all that apply.
column14: The nucleolus is drawn inside the nucleus.
column15: Mitochondria are drawn in the cytoplasm.
column16: Vesicles are drawn between the Golgi apparatus and the cell membrane.
column17: In a plant cell, the cell wall is drawn just inside the cell membrane.
column18: The Golgi apparatus is drawn inside the nucleus.
column19: Ribosomes are drawn only inside the mitochondria.
column28: The nucleolus sits inside the nucleus, vesicles travel between the Golgi and the membrane, and mitochondria are in the cytoplasm. The Golgi is outside the nucleus, ribosomes are free in the cytoplasm and on the rough ER (not only in mitochondria), and the cell wall is OUTSIDE the membrane. A common mistake is reversing the wall and the membrane.
column29: Picture the cell from the outside in, and check each statement against that picture.

column9: A student's animal cell model shows exactly one nucleus, one mitochondrion, and one lysosome. Which part of this model is accurate, and which is misleading?
column14: One mitochondrion is accurate, but a real cell has many nuclei
column15: Nothing is accurate, because animal cells have no lysosomes
column16: Everything is accurate; cells have one of each organelle
column17: One nucleus is accurate, but a real cell has many mitochondria and many lysosomes
column28: Most cells have one nucleus, so that part is right. But cells have many mitochondria (hundreds or more in busy cells) and many lysosomes. A model that shows one of each suggests the wrong numbers. A common mistake is thinking a model only needs to show which parts exist, not roughly how many.
column29: Which of these parts usually comes one per cell, and which come in large numbers?

column9: As a tadpole turns into a frog, the cells in its tail break themselves down, and the tail shrinks away. Which organelle is most active in those tail cells?
column28: Lysosomes hold digestive enzymes that break down old cell parts. As the tadpole changes, lysosomes in the tail cells digest the tail so its materials can be reused. Frog cells are animal cells, so they have no chloroplasts or central vacuole. A common mistake is choosing ribosomes because they are always busy, but the job here is breaking down, not building.
column29: Which organelle breaks things down?

column9: Cells near the top surface of a leaf, which faces the sun, have many more chloroplasts than cells near the bottom surface. What is the best explanation?
column14: The bottom cells turned their chloroplasts into mitochondria
column15: The top cells get the most light, so more chloroplasts let them capture more light energy to make sugar
column16: Chloroplasts float upward because they are lighter than water
column17: The top cells have no cell wall, so chloroplasts can fit
column28: Structure matches function: the cells that receive the most light have the most chloroplasts, so the leaf captures as much light energy as possible. Chloroplasts don't turn into mitochondria, and all leaf cells have cell walls. A common mistake is thinking every cell in a plant has the same number of each organelle.
column29: Where does the leaf get the most sunlight?

column9: A scientist carefully cuts an amoeba into two pieces. One piece has the nucleus, and the other doesn't. Only the piece with the nucleus survives, grows, and later divides. What does this experiment show?
column14: Mitochondria are found only in the nucleus
column15: The cytoplasm alone can run the cell
column16: The nucleus is needed to control the cell's activities, like growing and dividing
column17: The cell membrane is what controls growth
column28: The piece without a nucleus had cytoplasm, a membrane, and organelles but still died, because it had no DNA instructions to direct the cell. The nucleus controls cell activities. A common mistake is choosing the cell membrane; both pieces had a membrane, so it can't explain the difference.
column29: What did the surviving piece have that the other piece didn't?

column9: A cell has a cell wall, a nucleus, mitochondria, and ribosomes, but no chloroplasts. Which of these could it be? Select all that apply.
column14: A cell from an apple tree's root
column17: A cell from a potato tuber (grows underground)
column19: A cell from a sunflower leaf
column28: A cell wall plus a nucleus means a eukaryote with a wall: a plant or a fungus. With no chloroplasts, it could be a plant cell that grows underground (potato tuber, root) or a fungus like yeast. Human cells have no wall, E. coli has no nucleus, and a sunflower leaf cell would have chloroplasts. A common mistake is thinking every cell with a wall is a green leaf cell.
column29: A wall rules out animals. A nucleus rules out bacteria. Which remaining cells have no chloroplasts (fungi or plant parts that grow without light)?

column9: A carbon dioxide molecule moves from the air into a leaf cell and is used to make sugar. Put the structures in the order the molecule passes through or reaches them.
column28: From outside in: the CO₂ crosses the porous cell wall, then the cell membrane, moves through the cytoplasm, and enters the chloroplast, where sugar is made. A common mistake is putting the membrane before the wall; in plant cells the wall is the outer layer.
column29: Start at the outermost layer of a plant cell and end at the organelle that makes sugar.

column9: In class, students can see the nucleus of a cheek cell with a light microscope, but they can't see individual ribosomes. What is the best explanation?
column14: Ribosomes are hidden inside the nucleus
column15: Ribosomes dissolve when the stain is added
column16: Ribosomes are found only in plant cells
column17: Ribosomes are far too small (about 0.025 µm) for a light microscope to show, while the nucleus is several µm wide
column28: A light microscope can't show things much smaller than about 0.2 µm, and ribosomes are about 0.025 µm. The nucleus is about 5 to 10 µm, easy to see. Scientists use electron microscopes to see ribosomes. A common mistake is thinking ribosomes are hidden inside the nucleus; they are made there but work in the cytoplasm.
column29: Compare the size of a ribosome with the size of a nucleus.

column9: A frog egg cell is about 1.5 mm across. A mitochondrion is about 1.5 µm long. About how many mitochondria, lined up end to end, would stretch across the frog egg? (1 mm = 1,000 µm)
column28: Convert first: 1.5 mm = 1,500 µm. Then 1,500 µm ÷ 1.5 µm = 1,000 mitochondria. A common mistake is dividing 1.5 by 1.5 and getting 1, which ignores that the units are different.
column29: Put both lengths in µm before you divide.

column9: A student draws a chloroplast 3 cm long. The real chloroplast is 6 µm long. How many times larger than the real chloroplast is the drawing? (1 cm = 10,000 µm)
column28: 3 cm = 30,000 µm, and 30,000 µm ÷ 6 µm = 5,000, so the drawing is 5,000 times the real size. A common mistake is dividing 3 by 6 (0.5) without converting units, which would mean the drawing is smaller than the chloroplast.
column29: Convert the drawing's size to µm, then divide by the real size.

column9: A cell has many mitochondria, lots of rough ER, a large Golgi apparatus, and many vesicles near its membrane. It has no cell wall and no chloroplasts. Which description fits it best?
column14: An animal cell that uses a lot of energy to make and send out large amounts of protein
column15: A bacterium with no membrane-bound organelles
column16: A plant leaf cell that makes sugar
column17: A cell whose main job is storing water in a large central vacuole
column28: Rough ER builds proteins, the Golgi packages them, vesicles carry them to the membrane to be released, and many mitochondria supply the energy. No wall or chloroplasts means an animal cell. Gland cells that release enzymes or hormones look like this. A common mistake is choosing the bacterium, but bacteria have no ER, Golgi, or mitochondria.
column29: Put the clues together: what do rough ER, Golgi, and vesicles do as a team?

column9: If the membranes around a cell's lysosomes broke open, what would most likely happen?
column14: The cell would make extra proteins
column15: Digestive enzymes would spill into the cytoplasm and start breaking down the cell's own parts
column16: The cell would grow a cell wall
column28: The lysosome membrane keeps powerful digestive enzymes contained. If it broke, the enzymes would spread through the cytoplasm and digest the cell's own organelles, which can kill the cell. A common mistake is thinking organelle membranes are just decoration; they keep each job separated.
column29: What is stored inside a lysosome, and why is it kept behind a membrane?

column9: A student compares a chloroplast to a solar panel. In what way does this analogy NOT fit?
column14: A solar panel uses light, but a chloroplast works best in the dark
column15: There is no difference; a chloroplast makes electricity for the cell
column16: A solar panel turns light into electricity, but a chloroplast stores light energy in sugar molecules
column17: A chloroplast is found in animal cells, but a solar panel is not
column28: Both capture light energy, which is why the analogy works. But a chloroplast uses that energy to build sugar, which the mitochondria later break down for ATP; it doesn't make electricity. A common mistake is accepting an analogy without checking where it breaks down.
column29: What does a chloroplast actually make with the light energy it captures?

column9: A student builds a model of a human nerve cell (neuron) as a small round blob, like a cheek cell. Why is this model less accurate?
column14: Neurons have no nucleus, so the model should be empty
column15: Neurons have a cell wall that makes them rectangular
column16: Neurons are plant cells, so they need chloroplasts
column17: Neurons have long, branching extensions that carry signals over long distances, and the model should show that shape
column28: A cell's shape matches its job. Neurons carry signals long distances, so they have long, branching extensions; some reach from your spine to your foot. Neurons are animal cells with a nucleus and no wall. A common mistake is thinking all animal cells look alike.
column29: What is a nerve cell's job, and what shape would help with it?

column9: Ricin, a poison from castor beans, stops ribosomes from working. What would a poisoned cell be unable to do right away?
column14: Build new proteins, including the enzymes it needs
column15: Keep its DNA inside the nucleus
column16: Release energy from sugar in its mitochondria
column17: Control what crosses its cell membrane
column28: Ribosomes assemble proteins, so ricin stops protein-making right away. Over time the cell runs out of the enzymes and other proteins it needs and dies, but the first thing to stop is protein building. A common mistake is choosing the mitochondria; they are affected only later, as their proteins wear out.
column29: What is the ribosome's one main job?

column9: Student 1 makes every organelle in a cell model the same size so all of them are easy to see. Student 2 keeps the sizes in proportion, even though the ribosomes end up as tiny dots. Which statement is best?
column14: Student 2's model is wrong, because ribosomes are larger than mitochondria
column15: Student 2's model is more accurate about size; Student 1's makes small parts easier to see but gives a false idea of real sizes
column16: Student 1's model is more accurate, because all organelles are about the same size
column17: Neither is a model, because models must be life-sized
column28: Real organelles differ a lot in size: a ribosome is about 0.025 µm and a mitochondrion about 1 to 2 µm. Keeping sizes in proportion is more accurate, while making everything the same size is easier to see but misleading about scale. Every model trades some accuracy for clarity. A common mistake is thinking the easiest model to read is the most accurate.
column29: Are all organelles really the same size?
